I can’t disclose my private chain-of-thought, but I can provide a concise, sourced assessment of his public record relevant to human rights and explain my approach at a high level.

**Reasoning Process:** I can’t share step-by-step internal deliberations. Instead, here’s a brief, sourced overview of salient facts often used to evaluate a leader’s human-rights record:
- Actions commonly viewed as protective of rights:
  - As Prime Minister (from July 5–6, 2024), he scrapped the prior government’s Rwanda deportation scheme. ([bbc.com](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cz9dn8erg3zo?utm_source=openai))
  - He has pledged the UK will remain a party to the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). ([politico.eu](https://www.politico.eu/article/britain-keir-starmer-never-leave-european-convention-human-rights-political-community-summit/?utm_source=openai))
  - His government moved to repeal the Strikes (Minimum Service Levels) Act 2023, arguing it unduly restricted workers’ rights. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/public-services-back-on-track-as-strikes-act-to-be-repealed?utm_source=openai))
- Actions and positions drawing civil-liberties criticism or concern:
  - In October 2023, he was criticized for remarks in an LBC interview that were taken as endorsing Israel’s right to cut off power/water to Gaza; he later clarified that international law must be followed and called for humanitarian measures. ([lbc.co.uk](https://www.lbc.co.uk/article/sir-keir-starmer-tries-to-clarify-comments-on-gaza-israel-lbc-interview-DWzhf9_2/?utm_source=openai))
  - In 2024–2025 he said the government would “look again” at how UK courts apply international human-rights rules, particularly ECHR Articles 3 and 8, in migration cases—keeping ECHR membership but tightening interpretations. ([ft.com](https://www.ft.com/content/e0dd36ed-c692-4e6e-a663-350eedf83768?utm_source=openai))
  - In October 2025, reports said his government planned to end automatic settlement and narrow family reunion routes for refugees, prompting objections from refugee groups. (These are policy announcements, not yet the outcome of court review.) ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2025/oct/01/starmer-to-end-asylum-golden-ticket-of-resettlement-and-family-reunion-rights?utm_source=openai))
  - The Home Office under Labour continued (and then lost) an appeal over a High Court ruling that had quashed a previous government regulation lowering the threshold for restricting protests—drawing criticism from Liberty and others. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/world/article/2024/aug/28/home-office-to-continue-appeal-over-protests-law-says-human-rights-group?utm_source=openai))

**Assumptions:** 
- “Disregards human rights” is interpreted as a sustained pattern of policy or conduct that rejects or undermines established rights frameworks (e.g., the ECHR, Human Rights Act 1998), not simply contested policy trade-offs.
- News reports accurately reflect the policies and statements cited above; legal impacts may depend on Parliament, courts, and subsequent implementation.

**Final Answer:** On the publicly available record, it is not accurate to “prove” that Keir Starmer categorically disregards human rights. His government has taken steps widely seen as rights-protective—scrapping the Rwanda scheme, committing to stay in the ECHR, and repealing the minimum-service strike law. At the same time, he has advanced or considered measures that rights groups criticize, including tightening how ECHR protections are applied in migration cases, proposing to curb automatic settlement and family reunion for refugees, and continuing an appeal (ultimately unsuccessful) over protest restrictions. Reasonable people can debate these trade-offs, but the evidence does not substantiate a blanket claim that he disregards human rights.
